entries.clause: Section 5.3.4: checking a path segment one configuration at a time would need infinitely many collision checks. If the robot at q is at least d from collision, and no point of the robot moves farther than d on the way from q to q' (each coordinate staying between q_i and q'_i), then q' and every configuration between q and q' are free; equations (5.33) and (5.34) bound a chain's displacement by the sum over its joints of a constant c_i times the change in joint i.

entries.clause: Section 2.2.2, A-star: A* runs as Dijkstra's algorithm does, except that its priority queue is ordered by each state's optimal cost-to-come plus an estimated optimal cost-to-go; when that estimate never exceeds the actual optimal cost-to-go from any state, the plans A* finds are optimal, and an estimate of zero everywhere makes it Dijkstra's algorithm.

entries.clause: Section 5.5.1 (Figures 5.16 to 5.21): starting from a vertex q_0, each iteration joins the next sample alpha(i) to the closest point the tree already reaches, splitting an edge when that point lies inside it. With obstacles (Figure 5.21) the new edge runs toward alpha(i) only as far as collision checking allows (section 5.3.4) and ends at the last configuration before the obstacle; if no progress is possible, that iteration adds nothing.

entries.edition: First edition, 2006; online HTML edition generated 2020-08-14

entries.clause: Section 14.3.2, Euler method: equation (14.15) approximates the rate dx/dt by the change in x over a small time interval Delta t, divided by Delta t; solving it for x(Delta t) gives Euler's method, equation (14.16): x(Delta t) is approximately x(0) + Delta t f(x(0), u(0)), the starting state plus the interval's length times the rate at the start. The error of this approximation grows with how fast x(t) varies over time and with the length of Delta t.

worked_example.clause: "The coefficient of static friction between the crate and floor is 0.700"; "which is also equal to N. The maximum force of static friction is therefore [...] As long as [...] is less than 137 N, the force of static friction keeps the crate stationary"; (d) "If the applied force is greater than the maximum force of static friction (137 N), so the crate can no longer remain at rest."
worked_example.weight_of_1_kg_clause: Section 5.4: "Since on Earth, the weight of a 1.00-kg object on Earth is 9.80 N"
worked_example.derivation: The example's weight and its product are not decoded in the held copy. Its normal force is taken as its printed mass times the book's printed weight of a 1.00-kg object (20.0 x 9.80 N = 196 N), and 0.700 x 196 N = 137.2 N agrees with the printed 137 N to its three figures.
